strengths: Original and timely conceptual synthesis: connecting tabular foundation models (TabPFN) with the martingale posterior (MGP) framework allows practitioners to extract coherent epistemic uncertainty for downstream scientific estimands without manual prior or likelihood elicitation.

Intellectually honest and rigorous treatment of theoretical conditions: the authors explicitly test whether TabPFN satisfies the martingale and almost conditionally identically distributed (a.c.i.d.) conditions (Section 3.2 and Appendix C/Figure 5), candidly highlighting departures while grounding the method's validity on empirical path stability and coverage diagnostics.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper tests TabMGP across 30 diverse setups (11 synthetic, 19 real-world) covering linear regression, binary logistic regression, and multiclass classification, evaluating both joint credible sets and marginal coverage against multiple established baselines (Bayesian bootstrap, Copula MGP, NUTS Bayes, and asymptotic normals).

Strong empirical performance and usability: TabMGP avoids the sensitive bandwidth hyperparameter tuning required by copula-based MGPs, maintains near-nominal frequentist coverage, and produces tighter credible sets in challenging small-n/p regimes.
weaknesses: Lack of formal theoretical guarantees: because TabPFN does not strictly satisfy the martingale or a.c.i.d. conditions, the existence of an almost sure limiting measure F_\infty is not proven, leaving the validity of the posterior to rely purely on empirical diagnostics.

Substantial computational cost: autoregressive forward sampling of TabPFN over hundreds of steps (e.g., N = n + 500) requires repeated transformer forward passes with an expanding context window, taking 70–200s per posterior sample, which is orders of magnitude slower than bootstrap or standard MCMC implementations.

Architectural scalability constraints: TabPFN inherently comes with hard context-length and feature-dimension limits (e.g., ~10,000 context tokens and small-to-moderate feature counts), which restricts TabMGP's applicability to larger or higher-dimensional tabular problems.

Heuristic modeling of covariates: because TabPFN only supplies the conditional predictive distribution Y | X, TabMGP relies on the empirical Bayesian bootstrap for X, which may fail to capture smooth continuous feature manifolds and can lead to ill-conditioned design matrices in high-dimensional or sparse categorical settings.

strengths: Compelling conceptual integration: The paper successfully bridges modern tabular foundation models (TabPFN) with the martingale posterior (MGP) and Bayesian predictive inference (BPI) framework. While foundation models excel at predictive performance, they do not inherently output epistemic uncertainty over scientific parameters of interest; TabMGP provides an elegant, prior-free simulation mechanism to extract posterior distributions over arbitrary loss-minimizing functionals.

Methodological honesty and thorough diagnostics: Rather than glossing over the theoretical hurdles, the authors explicitly acknowledge that TabPFN violates both the classical martingale property and the relaxed almost conditionally identically distributed (a.c.i.d.) condition. They substantiate their approach with principled empirical diagnostics, including path stability (scaled L1 convergence), posterior contraction, and frequentist coverage assessments.

Comprehensive empirical benchmark: The method is evaluated across 30 setups (11 synthetic and 19 real-world tabular datasets) across continuous, binary, and multiclass targets. TabMGP demonstrates consistent near-nominal frequentist coverage while producing tighter credible sets than standard baselines, especially in lower sample-to-dimension ratio regimes.
Clarity and presentation: The manuscript is well-written, with clear schematics (Figure 1), well-structured algorithms (Algorithm 1), and well-documented experimental details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Substantial computational latency: Generating draws from TabMGP requires iterative autoregressive rollouts via TabPFN. Producing 100 posterior draws requires substantial GPU compute (70s to 200s per sample, leading to hours of computation per dataset), which is significantly slower than NUTS (Bayes baseline) or analytical/bootstrap baselines. Discussing strategies to accelerate sampling (e.g., batched rollouts, KV caching, or surrogate forward steps) would improve practical utility.

Dependence on discrete empirical bootstrap for covariates: Forward sampling the covariates $x$ via the Bayesian bootstrap restricts new queries to the observed multiset of feature points. While inherited from Fong et al. (2023), this discretization could hinder performance in higher-dimensional covariate spaces or when modeling support differs from training data.

Absence of formal theoretical guarantees: Because TabPFN deviates from c.i.d. and a.c.i.d. conditions, asymptotic convergence to a well-defined limiting measure $F_\infty$ remains an empirical observation rather than a proved mathematical guarantee.

Limited evaluation of non-likelihood loss functionals: The experimental section focuses primarily on standard negative log-likelihood losses (least squares and cross-entropy), where classical Bayesian baselines already operate well. Demonstrating TabMGP on non-standard loss functions (e.g., asymmetric pinball/quantile loss or robust Tukey biweight loss) would further showcase the power of generalized Bayes functionals.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Bridging tabular foundation models (specifically TabPFN) with the martingale posterior (MGP) and Bayesian predictive inference framework is an interesting and timely direction, addressing the practical desire to extract parameter epistemic uncertainty without specifying bespoke likelihood-prior pairs.
Extensive empirical benchmarking: The authors evaluate TabMGP across 30 diverse synthetic and real-world datasets spanning linear, binary logistic, and multiclass logistic regression models.

Strong empirical coverage: On real-world datasets, TabMGP demonstrates robust frequentist coverage and relatively compact joint credible sets, frequently matching or outperforming standard Bayesian bootstrap and copula-based predictive updates.

Transparent reporting of theoretical discrepancies: Rather than ignoring the failure of formal assumptions, the authors explicitly test and acknowledge that TabPFN violates both the traditional martingale property and the almost conditionally identically distributed (a.c.i.d.) condition, motivating the need for weaker theoretical foundations.
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical grounding: The foundational premise of the martingale posterior framework is the existence of a well-defined almost-sure limiting measure F_infinity, ensured by exchangeability, c.i.d., or a.c.i.d. conditions. Because TabPFN violates these conditions, there is no formal theoretical guarantee that the infinite predictive sequence converges or that the posterior samples are asymptotically valid. While the paper asserts that these conditions are sufficient rather than necessary, it provides no substitute theoretical justification or error bounds.

Ad-hoc handling of covariate distribution: Because TabPFN only models the conditional distribution Y | X, the method relies on the standard Bayesian bootstrap to sample future covariates X_{i+1} from the empirical distribution. This restricts future features to the exact discrete points observed in the sample, carrying over the well-known limitations of discrete predictive rules in small-n settings despite utilizing a continuous foundation model for the responses.

Vulnerability to autoregressive rollout drift and context limits: Running TabPFN autoregressively for hundreds of forward steps (N = n + 500) forces the model to condition on long sequences of its own pseudo-observations. Autoregressive rollouts are prone to compounding distribution shifts and error accumulation, especially as sequence lengths approach or exceed the model's pre-trained context window distributions.

Unfair or suboptimal baseline configurations: The classical Bayesian baseline is implemented using an 'asymptotic approximation of the posterior as the prior' rather than standard weakly informative or shrinkage priors (e.g., standard normal or Cauchy), which likely penalizes Bayes in low-n synthetic setups. Additionally, the bandwidth hyperparameter for the Copula baseline was manually fixed to 0.8 rather than tuned via standard cross-validation, explaining its failure in the logistic regression tasks.

Significant computational overhead: Generating 100 posterior draws requires autoregressive sampling across multiple steps, taking 70s to 200s per sample (several hours in total on an Nvidia L40s GPU) for datasets with sample sizes as small as n = 20 to 100, which is considerably more expensive than standard MCMC (NUTS) or copula baselines.

strengths: Compelling conceptual connection: The paper bridges Prior-Data Fitted Networks (TabPFN), which are trained to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions, with the Martingale Posterior (MGP) framework. Using a pretrained tabular transformer as the predictive engine for loss-based parameter inference is a natural, elegant, and timely idea.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The authors test the method across 30 distinct setups (11 synthetic, 19 real-world regression and classification tasks, including multiclass settings) as well as semi-synthetic datasets, systematically evaluating frequentist coverage and credible set volume.

Empirical performance: TabMGP consistently achieves close to nominal 95% coverage while maintaining substantially tighter credible sets than copula-based MGP baselines and diffuse Bayesian baselines, while mitigating the severe undercoverage issues that plague the Bayesian bootstrap in small-n regimes.

Transparency regarding theoretical limitations: Rather than sweeping non-martingale behavior under the rug, the authors explicitly evaluate the almost conditionally identically distributed (a.c.i.d.) condition and the martingale property (Appendix C), showing that TabPFN deviates from these sufficient conditions, and instead propose practical path-stability diagnostics to monitor convergence.
weaknesses: Absence of theoretical convergence guarantees: Because TabPFN violates both the exact martingale property and the a.c.i.d. condition, there is no mathematical guarantee that the sequence of predictive rules converges weakly to a well-defined limiting measure $F_\infty$. The foundational justification of the posterior remains heuristic and reliant on empirical diagnostics.

High computational overhead: Autoregressive forward sampling with a transformer over hundreds of rollout steps ($T = 500$) across $L = 100$ independent posterior trajectories is computationally demanding (taking 70–200 seconds per posterior sample). This significantly exceeds the runtime of standard Bayesian inference (NUTS) and classic bootstrapping.

Heuristic modeling of covariates: Because TabPFN only provides conditional distributions $Y \mid X$, future covariates $X_{i+1}$ are generated by resampling from the empirical distribution (the Bayesian bootstrap). When $n$ is very small, this restricts generated covariates to the observed sample points, limiting the diversity of synthesized data.

Narrow scope of evaluated estimands: Despite the MGP framework being designed for general loss-defined functionals $\theta(F)$, the empirical investigation is strictly limited to standard linear and logistic regression coefficients. Demonstrating inference on more general non-linear functionals or causal estimands (such as average treatment effects) would better demonstrate the unique utility of MGP over standard likelihood-based methods.

strengths: Innovative and timely conceptual bridge between tabular foundation models (prior-data fitted networks) and Bayesian predictive inference / martingale posteriors, providing a principled route to parameter uncertainty without likelihood elicitation.

Comprehensive empirical validation across 30 benchmark setups (synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world tabular data) spanning continuous, binary, and multiclass response settings, showing competitive coverage and compact credible sets relative to standard baselines.

Transparent investigation into theoretical validity: the authors empirically test both the martingale and almost conditionally identically distributed (a.c.i.d.) conditions, candidly showing that TabPFN violates them while demonstrating that empirical path stability and valid coverage are still achieved.

Eliminates practical bottlenecks of existing copula-based martingale posteriors, such as brittle bandwidth/hyperparameter tuning and manual symmetrisation for permutation invariance, while extending naturally to multiclass problems where copula baselines are inapplicable.
Clear, structured writing with thorough appendix investigations including trace plots, rollout sensitivity analysis, semi-synthetic data checks, and full marginal coverage tables.
weaknesses: Absence of formal theoretical guarantees: because TabPFN departs from both the martingale and a.c.i.d. conditions, there is currently no mathematical proof guaranteeing the existence of a unique limiting random measure F_\infty, leaving the justification largely empirical.

High computational overhead and context-length constraints: autoregressive forward sampling with TabPFN requires repeated model evaluations over hundreds of rollout steps (70s–200s per sample), and scaling to larger sample sizes is constrained by the transformer's maximum context length.

Asymmetric treatment of covariates: while the response y is modeled flexibly via TabPFN, the covariates x are drawn purely from the discrete Bayesian bootstrap, limiting the model's ability to explore unseen regions of the feature space.

Evaluation is restricted entirely to linear and generalized linear loss functionals (linear regression, binary and multinomial logistic regression), leaving the empirical behavior on more complex, nonlinear, or non-convex estimands unexamined.

strengths: Compelling conceptual synthesis: The paper makes a natural yet previously unexploited connection between tabular foundation models (TabPFN) and the martingale posterior (MGP) framework. Using TabPFN as a predictive engine allows practitioners to obtain epistemic uncertainty for arbitrary loss-defined functionals $\theta(F_\infty)$, addressing a key limitation of TabPFN.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The methodology is validated across 30 diverse setups (11 synthetic, 19 real-world) spanning linear, binary logistic, and multinomial logistic regression, complemented by semi-synthetic experiments. TabMGP consistently achieves near-nominal frequentist coverage with compact credible sets compared to baselines.

Pragmatic and thorough diagnostic toolkit: Given that deep neural networks cannot be formally verified to satisfy martingale or a.c.i.d. conditions, the authors develop practical empirical diagnostics (scaled $L_1$ convergence path stability, rollout depth sensitivity, and posterior contraction) that provide actionable guidance for practitioners.

Nuanced and transparent discussion: The manuscript is candid about the violation of classical sufficient conditions (martingale and a.c.i.d. properties), runtime constraints, and known failure modes (e.g., classification with very low $n/p$ ratios).
weaknesses: Absence of theoretical guarantees: Because TabPFN is demonstrated empirically to violate both the martingale and a.c.i.d. conditions, there is no formal guarantee that the forward-sampling empirical measure $F_N$ converges weakly to a well-defined random limiting measure $F_\infty$. While the authors justify this pragmatically, the theoretical underpinning of the resulting posterior remains open.

Substantial computational overhead: Autoregressive forward sampling through a transformer foundation model is computationally demanding (taking ~70s to 200s per posterior sample). Generating hundreds of posterior samples across long rollouts ($N = n + 500$) is markedly slower than traditional Bayesian or bootstrap alternatives.

Simplified covariate generation: Forward sampling of covariates $X$ relies on the empirical distribution (the Bayesian bootstrap), which restricts future feature draws strictly to observed feature values. In small-sample, high-dimensional regimes, this can limit the exploration of the feature space and exacerbate collinearity issues.

Scope of functionals: The empirical demonstration focuses exclusively on generalized linear models (linear, binary logistic, and multinomial logistic regression). Evaluating more complex, non-linear, or non-convex functionals would further strengthen the claims of general applicability.
